lead: The Raimondi and Boyd charts turn two numbers, the Sommerfeld number S and the length-to-diameter ratio L/D, into everything else a journal bearing design needs: how far off centre the journal sits, the thinnest oil film, the friction, the oil flow and, through a heat balance, the temperature rise. They exist because the film pressure in a bearing of finite length has no closed-form solution; it was solved numerically once and published as curves and tables. With the table for L/D = 1 and five minutes, you can check a bearing for a pump, a gearbox or a turbine.
prereq: You need: the Sommerfeld number from Chapter 5.4 and the minimum film thickness idea from Chapter 5.3.

blocks.text: Oil in a loaded journal bearing is dragged through a gap that narrows in the direction of rotation, and the Reynolds equation gives the pressure in that film. In a bearing of finite length oil also escapes at the two ends, so the pressure falls near each end, and that end effect rules out a clean formula. Raimondi and Boyd solved the equation by computer for a full 360° bearing and published the answers as curves against S, one curve for each L/D.

The input is the Sommerfeld number of Chapter 5.4, S = (μn/p)(r/c)², with μ in Pa·s at the film temperature, n in rev/s, p = W/(LD) in Pa and r/c the clearance ratio. The outputs, all dimensionless, are listed below for L/D = 1, the most common choice. Design data books print the same rows; between two rows, interpolate in proportion to S.

Read the columns like this. ε is the eccentricity ratio and h₀/c = 1 − ε the film thickness ratio. φ is the attitude angle between the load line and the line of centres. (r/c)f is the friction variable, so f = (r/c)f ÷ (r/c). Q/(rcnL) is the flow variable, the total oil pumped into the film. Q<sub>s</sub>/Q is the share of that flow that leaks out at the ends. p/p<sub>max</sub> gives the peak film pressure p<sub>max</sub> = p ÷ (p/p<sub>max</sub>). Notice the trend: as S falls, ε rises and the film thins.
The curves assume a steady load, a Newtonian oil of one viscosity, no misalignment and no oil groove inside the loaded arc. Break one of these and the chart value is a first guess, not the truth.

items: Fix L/D, usually between 0.5 and 1.5; L/D = 1 is the common first choice.
Compute S with the viscosity at the expected mean film temperature, not the tank temperature.
Read ε at that S on the curve for your L/D, and find h₀ = c(1 − ε), with c the radial clearance.
Read (r/c)f; then f = (r/c)f ÷ (r/c), the torque T = f W r and the power lost P<sub>f</sub> = 2πnT.
Read the flow variable; then Q = [Q/(rcnL)] × r c n L in m³/s. That sizes the supply.
Find the temperature rise from the heat balance below, and check h₀ and the temperature against the limits.

blocks.text: The heat balance assumes all the friction heat leaves in the oil flow: P<sub>f</sub> = ρ c<sub>p</sub> Q ΔT. Substitute the chart variables and the lengths cancel, leaving ΔT = 4π p (r/c)f ÷ [ρ c<sub>p</sub> × Q/(rcnL)]. For a typical mineral oil, ρ = 860 kg/m³ and c<sub>p</sub> = 1.76 kJ/(kg·K), so 4π/(ρc<sub>p</sub>) = 8.30 × 10⁻⁶ and, with p in MPa:

blocks.where: ΔT is the oil temperature rise in °C, p the bearing pressure in MPa, (r/c)f and Q/(rcnL) the chart readings. Some texts divide by (1 − ½ Q<sub>s</sub>/Q) as well, on the view that the side leakage leaves at the mean temperature; that gives a larger ΔT, so state which form you use.

sections.h3: The temperature loop and the limits

blocks.text: The charts were drawn for one viscosity, yet the oil that carries the load also heats up, and hot oil is thinner. So the last step feeds back into the first. Take the inlet temperature, add half of ΔT for the mean film temperature, look up the viscosity there and recompute S. Read the table again. Two passes usually settle it.

Two checks close the design. The film must be thicker than the combined roughness and the dirt that passes the filter; a widely used rule (Trumpler) asks for h₀ ≥ 0.005 + 0.00004 D, in mm with D in mm. And the bearing metal runs hotter than the oil leaving it, so keep the outlet oil well below the oil's limit. The charts also lose accuracy at very high ε, above about 0.95, and in turbulent or heavily grooved bearings.

examples.question: The bearing of Chapter 5.4 has D = L = 50 mm, c = 0.05 mm, W = 10 kN, n = 25 rev/s and μ = 0.02 Pa·s, giving S = 0.03125. Using the L/D = 1 table, find ε, h₀, the friction coefficient, the friction power, the oil flow and the temperature rise. Is the film thick enough?
steps: Temperature rise: p = 4 MPa, so ΔT = 8.30 × 4 × 1.364/4.682 = 9.7 °C. Check by energy: 107.1 W ÷ (860 × 1760 × 7.316 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s) = 9.7 °C.
Film check: Trumpler asks for h₀ ≥ 0.005 + 0.00004 × 50 = 0.007 mm. The bearing gives 0.0074 mm, a pass with almost no margin. A thicker oil or a longer bearing raises S and the film.
examples.answer: ε ≈ 0.85, h₀ ≈ 7.4 μm, f ≈ 0.0027, friction power ≈ 107 W, Q ≈ 7.3 cm³/s and ΔT ≈ 9.7 °C. The film only just meets the 7 μm guide, so the design needs a thicker oil or a longer bearing.

traps: Feeding rpm into S. With n in rpm every table reading is wrong; 1500 rpm is 25 rev/s.
(r/c)f is not f. Divide by r/c (500 in the example) to get f = 0.00273.
Reading the wrong L/D curve. The same S on the L/D = 0.5 curve gives a different ε than on the L/D = 1 curve.
Using the diametral clearance in h₀ = c(1 − ε). That doubles the film thickness you report.
Assuming a larger S means a thinner film. It is the other way round: S = 0.121 gives ε = 0.6, S = 0.0446 gives ε = 0.8.

quiz.q: What two quantities do you need before opening the Raimondi and Boyd charts?
quiz.a: The Sommerfeld number S and the length-to-diameter ratio L/D.

quiz.q: Name four quantities the charts give for a full journal bearing.
quiz.a: Any four of: eccentricity ratio ε (or h₀/c), attitude angle φ, friction variable (r/c)f, flow variable Q/(rcnL), side-leakage ratio Q<sub>s</sub>/Q and the pressure ratio p/p<sub>max</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is there a separate curve for each L/D?
quiz.a: Side leakage at the two ends depends on bearing length. Two bearings with the same S but different L/D have different pressure fields, so ε, friction and flow all differ.

quiz.q: The table gives (r/c)f = 3.22 at S = 0.121. Why is the friction coefficient not 3.22?
quiz.a: The column is the friction coefficient multiplied by the clearance ratio r/c, which is several hundred. For r/c = 500, f = 3.22/500 = 0.00644.

quiz.q: At S = 0.121 and L/D = 1, the radial clearance is 0.04 mm. Find ε, h₀ and the film thickness ratio.
quiz.a: S = 0.121 is a table row: ε = 0.6, so h₀/c = 0.4 and h₀ = 0.4 × 0.04 = 0.016 mm = 16 μm.

quiz.q: A bearing with p = 2 MPa reads (r/c)f = 3.22 and Q/(rcnL) = 4.33. Find the oil temperature rise, taking all the heat into the oil flow.
A proposed bearing reads ε = 0.95. What is the risk, and what can you change?
quiz.a: The film is only 5 % of the clearance, close to the surface roughness, so metal contact is likely. Raise S with a more viscous oil, more length (lower p) or a lower running temperature through better cooling. Then recheck h₀ against the roughness rule.

quiz.q: Two students read different ε for the same bearing. Give two likely reasons.
quiz.a: They used different L/D curves; one put speed in rpm instead of rev/s; or they took viscosity at different oil temperatures.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern bearing design solves the Reynolds equation numerically for the actual groove and misalignment, and adds the energy equation so viscosity varies across the film, which is called thermohydrodynamic analysis. The printed charts survive as a quick check and as a way to see trends. Search "finite journal bearing Reynolds equation" and "thermohydrodynamic lubrication".
